props.title: Experiment Perilous
props.initialSlug: Gothic mystery stalks a beautiful woman in 1903 NYC

sections.content: Experiment Perilous (1944) stands as a fascinating psychological thriller from RKO's film noir golden age, sharing DNA with Gaslight (1944) and Rebecca (1940) in its Gothic atmosphere and exploration of psychological manipulation. Director Jacques Tourneur, fresh off his supernatural masterpiece Cat People (1942), brings his signature shadowy visual style to this adaptation of Margaret Carpenter's novel. The film follows Dr. Huntington Bailey (George Brent) as he becomes entangled with the mysterious Allida Bederaux (Hedy Lamarr), leading to a dangerous game of cat-and-mouse with her controlling husband Nick (Paul Lukas).

sections.content: The film showcases Tourneur's masterful command of atmosphere, using expressionistic lighting and deep shadows that rival contemporaries like The Spiral Staircase (1946) and Sorry, Wrong Number (1948). Cinematographer Tony Gaudio creates a claustrophobic Victorian world where danger lurks in every corner, particularly in the Bederaux mansion sequences. The period setting distinguishes it from many noir contemporaries, proving that psychological tension isn't confined to modern urban settings.

Hedy Lamarr delivers one of her finest performances as the trapped Allida, rivaling similar roles like Joan Fontaine in Suspicion (1941) and Gene Tierney in Dragonwyck (1946). The film's exploration of male control and psychological abuse feels remarkably modern, predating later examinations like Sleep, My Love (1948) and Sudden Fear (1952). sections.content: While often overlooked in noir discussions, Experiment Perilous masterfully blends Gothic romance with noir elements, creating a unique hybrid that influenced later psychological thrillers. Its combination of period setting, psychological manipulation, and noir visual style created a template followed by films like My Name Is Julia Ross (1945) and The Two Mrs. Carrolls (1947).
